question:
Rhombus \(ABCD\) is similar to rhombus \(BFDE.\) The area of rhombus \(ABCD\) is \(24,\) and \(\angle BAD = 60^\circ.\) What is the area of rhombus \(BFDE?\)

[Figure 1](figures/2006_AMC_12B_Q13_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The shared segment \(BD\) connects the two rhombuses. Finding which diagonal corresponds to it will reveal their scale factor.

[Figure 1](figures/2006_AMC_12B_Q13_question_fig1.svg)

Let \(u>0\) be the side length of \(ABCD\), and let \(M\) be the intersection of its diagonals. Since \(AB=AD=u\) and \(\angle BAD=60^\circ\), triangle \(ABD\) is equilateral. Thus \(BD=u\).

A rhombus's diagonals bisect each other perpendicularly, so \(BM=u/2\) and \(AM=AC/2\). Applying the Pythagorean theorem to right triangle \(ABM\) gives
\[
AM^2=u^2-\left(\frac u2\right)^2=\frac{3u^2}{4}.
\]
Therefore \(AC=2AM=\sqrt3u\).

The ordered similarity \(ABCD\sim BFDE\) matches \(A\) with \(B\) and \(C\) with \(D\). Consequently, diagonal \(AC\) of the first rhombus corresponds to diagonal \(BD\) of the second. The length scale factor from \(ABCD\) to \(BFDE\) is
\[
k=\frac{BD}{AC}=\frac{u}{\sqrt3u}=\frac1{\sqrt3}.
\]
Corresponding bases and heights both scale by \(k\), so areas scale by \(k^2\). Hence the requested area is
\[
24\left(\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)^2=\boxed{8},
\]
which is choice \(\mathrm{C}\).

edges.reason: Half-diagonals form right triangles, so Pythagoras helps recover a side when diagonal lengths are supplied. Area from two diagonals or side from perimeter needs no such calculation; retain the limited preparation link.
The stated rhombus properties include inherited parallelogram bisection of diagonals and opposite-side relationships.
edges.scope: rhombus as parallelogram; inherited diagonal bisection

edges.reason: Proportional corresponding sides are part of the similarity definition.
Similar polygons introduce a common side ratio. The node also covers curved regions and general similarities, so polygon criteria help but are not strictly necessary.
The triangle area-ratio property is a concrete instance of the general square law. The law can be justified by grid or dilation arguments for any region without triangle properties.
edges.scope: triangle special case of the square law

edges.reason: Distinguishing a squared area factor from the linear factor presupposes area as a two-dimensional size, separate from perimeter. Without it, the square law has no meaning.
The scale factor and the area factor are ratios of corresponding quantities. Applying or inverting k^2 needs ratios as quotients, which every method of this node uses.
